  "title": "Continuous Co-Evolution of Interpretable Problem Archives and Policy in RLVR via Online Quality-Diversity",
  "core_problem": "Self-evolving RLVR systems that iteratively generate and solve problems suffer from diversity collapse (Prism, Mar 2026) and diversity illusion (R-Diverse, Feb 2026). Recent work has made important progress: SwS (NeurIPS 2025) demonstrates that category-based weakness identification with proportional budget allocation and targeted synthesis yields +10% average improvement on 7B models. However, SwS operates as a static two-stage offline pipeline (preliminary RL → identify failures → synthesize 40K problems → augmented RL) that cannot adapt to the policy's evolving capability landscape during training. Similarly, Prism's 128 semantic clusters and R-Diverse's code-embedding repulsion maintain diversity reactively but cannot target specific gaps. The fundamental limitation shared by all existing approaches is the absence of continuous, quality-aware co-evolutionary pressure between the problem distribution and the learning policy: SwS identifies weaknesses once and generates a fixed augmentation set; Prism rewards rarity without quality filtering; R-Diverse repels repetition without maintaining the most learnable problems. How can we enable continuous online co-evolution where the problem archive dynamically reshapes around the policy's evolving capabilities, maintaining only maximally learnable problems per behavioral niche through iterative quality-based replacement?",
  "opportunity": "SwS (NeurIPS 2025) validates the core intuition that targeted synthesis for identified weaknesses substantially outperforms indiscriminate augmentation (+10%/+7.7% on 7B/32B). Prism (arXiv 2603.13309) demonstrates that structured diversity maintenance prevents collapse (+3.37 AIME 2024 over R-Zero on Qwen3-4B). R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103) shows that skill-aware diversity prevents surface diversity illusion (+6.46 AIME 2024 over R-Zero, 12.71→19.17 on Qwen3-4B). However, all three share critical limitations that create an opportunity for unified improvement: (1) SwS's offline pipeline cannot re-identify weaknesses as the policy improves—problems synthesized for early-training weaknesses become too-easy mid-training, wasting curriculum space; (2) Neither SwS nor Prism nor R-Diverse performs quality-based problem replacement—SwS generates once, Prism tracks coverage via EMA counts, R-Diverse appends to a growing memory bank; (3) None creates co-evolutionary pressure where the archive continuously reshapes around the policy. VCRL (arXiv 2509.19803) validates that moderate advantage variance signals optimal learnability, providing the principled replacement criterion. The 'sparse policy selection' finding (arXiv 2605.06241, May 2026) shows RL affects only 1-3% of tokens at high-entropy decision points—but critically, the 'Sharper Primitives' analysis (arXiv 2602.08281) demonstrates that diverse training activates and sharpens a broader range of latent primitives even under the selection hypothesis, supporting the value of comprehensive coverage. This opens a clear opportunity: continuous online co-evolution that unifies SwS's weakness targeting, Prism's coverage maintenance, and quality-based archive management into a single adaptive framework operating during live RLVR training.",
  "landscape": "**Weakness-driven targeted synthesis.** SwS (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.08989) is the most directly relevant prior work. It identifies model weaknesses as problems where accuracy never reaches 50% with negative slope during preliminary RL, groups failures by mathematical category (Algebra, Geometry, Precalculus, Number Theory, Counting & Probability), allocates synthesis budget proportionally to category failure rates (|X_T,D_i| = |X_T| · F_D_i / ΣF_D_j), and generates 40K targeted problems via concept extraction and recombination using LLaMA-3.3-70B with difficulty filtering [25%, 75%]. Results: +10.0% (7B), +7.7% (32B) average across 8 benchmarks; AIME 2024: 26.7 avg@1 on Qwen2.5-7B. Critical limitation: operates as a two-stage offline pipeline (Stage 1 RL → offline synthesis → Stage 2 RL) with no iterative adaptation—weaknesses identified once cannot update as the policy improves during Stage 2. STAT (arXiv 2510.10023) creates Missing-Skill-Profiles by monitoring student failures and synthesizes skill-targeted examples, achieving +7.5% on MATH via SFT—demonstrating the weakness→synthesis pattern in supervised settings. **Self-evolving problem generation for RLVR.** SvS (ICLR 2026) achieves +18.3%/+22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/25 via answer-preserving variational mutations. R-Zero (ICLR 2026) co-evolves Challenger+Solver via uncertainty targeting but collapses after iteration 3. **Diversity maintenance.** Prism (arXiv 2603.13309, Mar 2026) prevents collapse via 128 K-means semantic clusters with ZPD gate [0.5, 0.9] and rarity bonus, achieving AIME 2024: 16.77, AMC: 61.25, OlympiadBench: 45.58 on Qwen3-4B. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) introduces SAM (code→embedding skill diversity) + MAP (persistent memory bank with dual similarity penalties), achieving AIME 2024: 19.17 (4B), 24.48 (8B). **Verification approaches.** VHG (arXiv 2605.06660, May 2026) introduces three-party self-play with explicit verifier gating: setter reward = I[V(x,y*)=1] × (1-Acc_solver), preventing reward hacking where invalid problems appear difficult. Instantiates Hard (symbolic/SymPy) and Soft (LLM-based) verifiers. Directly relevant to our verification pipeline. **Error-analysis-driven generation.** 'Automatically Generating Hard Math Problems from Hypothesis-Driven Error Analysis' (arXiv 2604.04386, Apr 2026) uses AI-generated hypotheses to identify mathematical concepts LLMs struggle with, generating problems that reduce Llama-3.3-70B accuracy from 77% to 45%—demonstrating the weakness→targeted generation pattern for benchmarking. **Curriculum optimization.** SEC (arXiv 2505.14970) formulates curriculum selection as MAB over predefined categories using |advantage| as learning gain proxy. VCRL (arXiv 2509.19803) validates that reward variance follows an inverted-U relationship with learnability. **QD and archive-based approaches.** SPARQ (arXiv 2506.06499) demonstrated MAP-Elites for offline synthetic math generation. DéjàQ (arXiv 2601.01931) applies MAP-Elites during RL at GSM-Symbolic level with single-dimension archive. **Fundamental premise.** 'Sparse Policy Selection, Not Capability Learning' (arXiv 2605.06241, May 2026) shows RL modifies only 1-3% of tokens at high-entropy decision points, promoting tokens already in the base model's top-5. ReasonMaxxer matches full RL with 50 problems. However, 'New Skills or Sharper Primitives' (arXiv 2602.08281) demonstrates that diverse training activates broader latent primitive coverage even under the selection hypothesis—diverse curricula sharpen precision across a wider capability spectrum. 'Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity Beyond the Base Model?' (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2504.13837) finds >95% of RL-solved problems are solvable by base model at high pass@k, but RL dramatically improves sampling efficiency—supporting coverage-focused rather than capability-creation framing. **Other concurrent work.** ARISE (arXiv 2603.16060) co-evolves hierarchical skill libraries. GAR (arXiv 2510.11769) implements adversarial co-evolution for theorem proving. Vocabulary Dropout (arXiv 2604.03472) addresses diversity collapse via token-level perturbation. SAND-Math (arXiv 2507.20527) demonstrates competition-level synthesis at 37.7% survival. **The gap.** SwS demonstrates offline targeted synthesis works but cannot adapt online. Prism/R-Diverse maintain diversity reactively without quality filtering or targeted generation. VHG improves verification but not curriculum management. No existing work combines (a) continuous online weakness re-identification as the policy evolves, (b) quality-based archive replacement maintaining maximally learnable problems per niche, and (c) emergent curriculum dynamics where solve-rate recalibration creates automatic difficulty escalation during live RLVR training.",
  "inspired_by": "SwS_insight['category-based weakness targeting yields +10% over indiscriminate synthesis'] + Prism_insight['semantic coverage prevents collapse in self-evolving RLVR'] + R-Diverse_insight['code-embedding skill diversity prevents surface diversity illusion'] + VCRL_insight['moderate advantage variance indicates optimal learnability'] + sparse_policy_selection_insight['RL selects among existing primitives, so comprehensive coverage activation matters'] + sharper_primitives_insight['diverse training sharpens broader primitive range even without creating new capabilities']",
  "approach": "We propose QD-RLVR, which maintains a 2D MAP-Elites behavioral archive spanning difficulty (5 empirical solve-rate bins: [0-0.2, 0.2-0.4, 0.4-0.6, 0.6-0.8, 0.8-1.0]) × mathematical topic (algebra, geometry, number theory, combinatorics, probability) = 25 cells during online GRPO training. Unlike SwS's one-shot offline pipeline, QD-RLVR continuously co-evolves the archive with the policy, creating adaptive co-evolutionary pressure impossible in offline approaches.\n\n**Archive Initialization.** Seed with existing competition problems (AMC 10/12, AIME, Olympiad from NuminaMath-1.5 curated subsets and DeepScaleR). Topic classification via GPT-4o-mini (validated at 84-92% accuracy; arXiv 2411.00042). Difficulty via empirical solve-rate from 16 rollouts on the base policy. Each cell stores up to M=20 problems, giving maximum archive capacity of 500 problems.\n\n**Training Loop (GRPO on Qwen3-8B-Base, validated on Qwen3-32B-Base, VERL framework):**\n\n(a) **Adaptive ZPD Sampling.** Select training batch from archive cells where the policy's solve-rate lies in a learnable ZPD window [lo, hi] (initialized [0.2, 0.8]). Within-ZPD cells are weighted by learnability signal: moderate advantage variance from 8 GRPO rollouts, following VCRL's validated inverted-U relationship. This parallels SEC's MAB-based categorical sampling but integrates advantage-variance with archive structure.\n\n(b) **GRPO Policy Update.** Standard GRPO step with 8 rollouts per problem, binary correctness reward verified via math-verify.\n\n(c) **Staggered Archive Refresh (every K=50 steps).** To manage computational overhead, we employ lazy evaluation: re-evaluate only cells that were sampled in the last K steps (typically 40-60% of archive, ~200-300 problems × 8 rollouts = 1600-2400 rollouts) rather than all 500 problems. Problems crossing bin boundaries are reassigned. Cells where all problems have solve-rate >0.9 (mastered) or <0.1 (too hard) are flagged as stale. Estimated overhead: ~20-25% of training compute per refresh cycle (1600-2400 evaluation rollouts + synthesis rollouts vs ~12,800 training rollouts per 50 steps at batch_size=32×8). We discuss overhead reduction strategies in ablation A7.\n\n(d) **Online Targeted Synthesis (every K=50 steps).** For under-populated (<5 problems) or stale cells, generate problems targeting specific behavioral descriptors. KEY DISTINCTION FROM SwS: weakness re-identification happens continuously—a cell that was well-populated at step 100 may become stale (all problems mastered) by step 500, triggering new synthesis for that specific niche. This creates emergent curriculum escalation impossible in SwS's static pipeline.\n\nHybrid verification pipeline:\n  - *VHG-inspired validity gating*: separate validity verification from difficulty assessment, preventing invalid problems from inflating difficulty estimates\n  - *Answer-preserving mutation* (SvS-style) when seed problems exist in the cell (~near-100% validity)\n  - *math-verify + majority voting* (16 rollouts, ≥75% consistency threshold) for newly generated problems\n  - *5× overgeneration budget*: generate 5 candidates per slot, select the valid one with highest learnability signal\n  - *Expected validity*: ~47% per attempt at competition level (SAND-Math evidence), yielding >90% probability of ≥1 valid candidate per 5× batch\n\n(e) **Quality-Based Archive Replacement.** New valid problems replace existing cell occupants ONLY when they yield higher learnability signal (moderate advantage variance). This creates continuous co-evolutionary pressure absent in all prior work: SwS generates once without replacement; Prism tracks counts without quality filtering; R-Diverse appends without eviction. The archive thus maintains the MOST LEARNABLE problems per niche at any given training stage.\n\n(f) **Solve-rate Recalibration and Emergent Curriculum.** After policy improvement, problems naturally shift to easier bins. A problem in 'hard number theory' (solve-rate 0.15) at step 100 may become 'medium number theory' (solve-rate 0.45) by step 300, vacating the hard cell and triggering new hard synthesis. This creates automatic difficulty escalation without explicit scheduling—a capability that SwS's static problem set fundamentally cannot provide.\n\n**Addressing the Sparse Policy Selection Challenge:**\nThe finding that RL affects only 1-3% of tokens (arXiv 2605.06241) does not undermine our approach. Following the 'Sharper Primitives' framework (arXiv 2602.08281), we reframe QD-RLVR's goal: comprehensive COVERAGE of latent reasoning primitives rather than capability creation. The MAP-Elites archive ensures systematic activation of primitives across all topic×difficulty combinations, sharpening precision across the full capability spectrum. Under this framing, archive diversity directly increases the range of high-entropy decision points where RL can provide useful signal. We include an empirical test: measure the correlation between archive cell coverage and per-cell pass@k improvement to validate that broader primitive activation (not just sampling efficiency on seen problems) drives gains.\n\n**Key differentiators vs prior work:**\n- *vs SwS*: (a) Continuous online co-evolution vs one-shot offline pipeline—weaknesses are re-identified every 50 steps as the policy evolves, not frozen from preliminary training; (b) quality-based archive replacement vs one-shot generation—only maximally learnable problems survive; (c) emergent curriculum via solve-rate recalibration vs static augmentation set; (d) MAP-Elites archive structure vs proportional budget allocation without persistent management\n- *vs Prism*: (a) Explicit interpretable behavioral cells vs opaque 128 semantic clusters; (b) quality-based replacement vs EMA-smoothed count tracking; (c) targeted synthesis for identified gaps vs rarity bonus for under-represented clusters; (d) adaptive difficulty binning vs static embedding partition\n- *vs R-Diverse*: (a) Proactive gap-filling vs reactive similarity repulsion; (b) interpretable topic×difficulty structure vs continuous code-embedding space; (c) quality-filtered archive vs append-only growing memory bank\n\n**Ablations:**\n(A1) 3D archive adding GPT-4-extracted procedural skills (~117 clusters from Didolkar et al., NeurIPS 2024, 94%+ relevance), yielding ~100+ cells\n(A2) Code-embedding diversity (R-Diverse SAM-style) as alternative to explicit topic labels within archive cells\n(A3) SEC-style MAB sampling vs ZPD-frontier sampling over archive cells\n(A4) Quality-based replacement vs random replacement vs no replacement (isolates co-evolutionary contribution)\n(A5) Online continuous refresh vs SwS-style offline two-stage (isolates online adaptation contribution)\n(A6) 2D vs 1D (difficulty-only, topic-only) archives\n(A7) Refresh frequency: K=25 vs K=50 vs K=100 steps, and lazy vs full evaluation (overhead-performance tradeoff)\n(A8) Archive coverage vs per-cell pass@k correlation (tests sparse-selection-compatible justification)",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MISSING WORK: CLPO (arXiv 2509.25004) creates an online curriculum during RLVR using real-time difficulty assessment with Adaptive Problem Restructuring that diversifies medium-difficulty problems and simplifies hard ones. Achieves 50.0% on AIME 2024 with Qwen3-8B. While mechanistically different (no persistent archive), it addresses the same 'adaptive online curriculum during RLVR' problem and should be discussed as related work.", "MISSING WORK: MathForge/DGPO (arXiv 2601.20614, ICLR 2026) introduces Difficulty-Aware GRPO with Multi-Aspect Question Reformulation—directly relevant as it modifies GRPO's optimization to handle difficulty-aware training and reformulates problems to increase difficulty/diversity. An ICLR 2026 paper in the same space cannot be omitted.", "MISSING WORK: AdaRFT (arXiv 2504.05520) dynamically adjusts training problem difficulty based on recent reward signals, evaluated on AMC/AIME/IMO-style problems with 2× training speedup. CPMobius (arXiv 2602.02979) implements cooperative Coach-Player co-evolution for data-free RL with targeted problem generation. AERO (arXiv 2602.03084) uses ZPD-based autonomous evolutionary reasoning. OpenSIR (arXiv 2511.00602) optimizes for both difficulty and diversity in self-improving reasoning. All are relevant concurrent works.", "UNDERSTATED OVERLAP WITH DéjàQ: The proposal characterizes DéjàQ as 'MAP-Elites during RL at GSM-Symbolic level with single-dimension archive' but underemphasizes that DéjàQ already implements the two most-claimed contributions: (1) online co-evolution during RL training and (2) quality-based archive replacement (f(x')>f(y) → replace). The true delta over DéjàQ is narrower than presented: competition-level scaling + 2D interpretable archive + SwS-style continuous weakness targeting. This delta should be articulated more precisely.", "EMERGENT CURRICULUM CLAIM NEEDS GROUNDING: The 'emergent curriculum via solve-rate recalibration' mechanism—where problems shift to easier bins as policy improves, vacating hard cells—is intuitive but unvalidated. With only 25 cells and 20 problems per cell, the dynamics may be too coarse for meaningful emergent curriculum effects. CLPO's finer-grained online difficulty assessment (per-problem accuracy thresholds) may achieve smoother curriculum adaptation.", "COMPETITION-LEVEL ARCHIVE POPULATION UNCERTAINTY: The 25-cell archive requires populating cells like 'hard number theory' or 'hard combinatorics' with 20 valid competition-level problems each. Even with 5× overgeneration and SAND-Math-level survival rates (~37.7%), the most specific cells (e.g., hard geometry with solve-rate 0-0.2) may take many synthesis cycles to populate with genuinely valid and diverse problems, potentially leaving systematic archive gaps."]
Feedback: The proposal has matured significantly through three rounds but needs to address a new class of issues: missing concurrent works and understated overlap with DéjàQ.

Priority revisions:

(1) **Add CLPO and MathForge as related work.** CLPO (arXiv 2509.25004) is the most relevant omission—it creates an online adaptive curriculum during RLVR with problem restructuring, achieving 50% on AIME 2024 with Qwen3-8B. MathForge (arXiv 2601.20614, ICLR 2026) does difficulty-aware GRPO with question reformulation. Neither uses persistent archives, so argue that archive-based management provides interpretability and systematic coverage that per-batch restructuring cannot.

(2) **Sharpen the delta over DéjàQ.** DéjàQ already does online MAP-Elites + quality-based replacement during RL training. AdaRFT (Adaptive Curriculum Reinforcement Finetuning) is a method that significantly improves both the efficiency and final accuracy of RFT through adaptive curriculum learning.

## AERO: Autonomous Evolutionary Reasoning Optimization via Endogenous Dual-Loop Feedback

AERO is an unsupervised framework that achieves autonomous reasoning evolution by internalizing self-questioning, answering, and criticism within a synergistic dual-loop system.

### Key Innovation

The paper was published on February 4, 2026 (arXiv:2602.03084). The framework addresses challenges with Large Language Models that remain bottlenecked by reliance on expert-annotated data and external verifiers.

### ZPD and Zone of Proximal Development

Inspired by the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) theory, AERO utilizes entropy-based positioning to target the "solvability gap" and employs Independent Counterfactual Correction for robust verification. # CLPO: Comprehensive Technical Extraction

## 1. METHODOLOGY

### Online Curriculum Learning (Real-time Difficulty Assessment)
The framework generates G rollouts per problem and computes empirical accuracy:
- **Accuracy Metric**: "Acc(q,πθ)=1/G ∑ I(Verifier(yi,a)=True)" 
- **Difficulty Thresholds**: Default (τhard, τmed) = (0.3, 0.7)
- **Partitioning Strategy**:
  - Hard: Acc(q) ≤ 0.3
  - Medium: 0.3 < Acc(q) ≤ 0.7
  - Easy: Acc(q) > 0.7 (excluded from restructuring)

### Adaptive Problem Restructuring (APR)
Two targeted approaches based on difficulty:

**Medium Problems (Diversification)**:
- "semantically equivalent but varied phrasings" to enhance robustness
- Goal: "grasp deeper semantic commonalities"

**Hard Problems (Simplification)**:
- "generate a restructured problem q′ that is easier for the model"
- "transform an initially intractable problem into effective training signal"

Both preserve original answer strictly.

### Value-Driven Filtering
Two-stage construction of final training batch Bmix:

1. **Base Set**: 0 < Acc(q,πθ) < 1 from original batch
2. **Restructured Set**: Same accuracy criterion applied post-restructuring
3. **Final Batch**: Union of both sets

### Difficulty-Aware Policy Optimization
Dynamic KL regularization via scaling factor λd:
- λhard = 0.3 (fewer constraints on hard problems)
- λnon-hard = 1.0 (stronger constraints on easier problems)
- Effective coefficient: βeff(q,πθ) = λd·β

This allows "greater policy exploration on difficult problems while enforcing stronger regularization" on mastered ones.

|-----------|------|------|---------------|------|

| GPQA Diamond | 62.63% | 48.48% | 50.50% | 47.80% |
| MMLU Pro | 72.39% | 70.01% | 70.98% | 69.86% |

- Batch size: 64
- Learning rate: 1e-6 (constant)
- Temperature: 1.0
- Max response length: 8192 tokens
- Hardware: 8× NVIDIA H20 GPUs

**No persistent archive between steps**. The framework operates fully online:
- Each training step evaluates current batch with current policy
- Difficulty classifications are real-time and discarded after batch construction
- Restructured problems exist only for single training iteration
- No problem history or performance memory maintained

- CLPO solves: wasted compute on mastered problems and failures on extremely hard ones

- Minerva-Math: +22.8 points

- AIME2024: +3.3 points
- DAPO wins only on in-domain MATH-500 (-1.6 points)

CLPO competitive/superior without external models:
- "guidance signal is derived entirely from introspection on own online performance"
- Eliminates need for GPT-4o or offline expert trajectories
- Achieves comparable or better results

**Difficulty Range Impact** (Figure 3, right):
- Too wide (0.125, 0.875): Poor performance (hard problems treated as medium)
- Optimal (0.25, 0.75): Best results
- Too narrow (0.375, 0.625): Insufficient material at capability frontier

**Dynamic KL Scaling** (Figure 4):
- α = 0.3 (λhard): Optimal balance
- α = 0.5: Worst performance ("suboptimal exploration range")
- α = 0.8, 1.0: Overly restrictive
- α = 0.1: "compromise stability through insufficient constraint"

**Restructuring Strategy** (Figure 3, left):
- Medium-only diversification: Better than hard-only simplification
- Combined approach: Optimal ("most comprehensive capability improvement")

Acknowledged by authors:

1. **Difficulty Assessment**: "relies primarily on final answer correctness; future work could explore incorporating more fine-grained process signals"

2. **Domain Specificity**: Method "primarily validates in domain of mathematical reasoning"; extending to code generation and scientific QA remains unexplored

3. **Scalability**: "adaptive learning capabilities will exhibit even greater potential as training data and model parameter scales continue to grow" (validation pending)

4. **External Restructuring**: Adaptive Problem Restructuring itself requires LLM generation (computational cost not quantified)

# Technical Details of DéjàQ: Complete Specification

## MAP-Elites Implementation

**Archive Structure:**
DéjàQ maintains a discretized grid-based archive where "each item is assigned a feature descriptor via a mapping d:𝒳→ℝⁿ" and "the feature space is discretised into a finite grid by assuming that each dimension of d(x) is categorical."

**Behavioral Descriptors:**
The system uses a single categorical dimension: **problem setting**. Eight setting categories are employed: Personal Life, Professional, Economic, Recreational, Events, Scientific, Technical, and Environmental. Each problem is classified into exactly one setting category via LLM-assisted inspection.

**Archive Population:**
Initial seeding uses "all templates from GSM-Symbolic" (mirzadeh2024gsmsymbolic), which are then classified and stored in corresponding cells based on their setting descriptor.

## Quality-Based Replacement Criterion

**Fitness Function:**
Learnability serves as the sole fitness metric: "l_θ(x) = p_θ(x)(1−p_θ(x))" where p_θ(x) denotes the probability the model solves problem x correctly.

**Replacement Logic:**
"If the cell is empty or if f(x′)>f(y), then x′ replaces y in the archive." For learnability specifically, a mutated candidate replaces the current cell occupant when its estimated learnability score exceeds the incumbent's score.

**Learnability Estimation:**
The system uses an "unbiased estimator l̂_θ(x) = (K/(K−1))p̂_θ(x)(1−p̂_θ(x))" computed from K=100 model completions per problem.

## Online Co-Evolution During RL Training

**Concurrent Process Architecture:**
Two asynchronous processes operate simultaneously sharing inference infrastructure:

1. **Training Loop (Student):** Samples batches from the archive using "a mixture of their estimated learnability (favouring higher values) and age (favouring more recent items)." Performs GRPO updates.

2. **Evolution Loop (Teacher):** Continuously selects high-quality parents, applies mutations, scores candidates via learnability, and updates archive cells when fitness improves.

**Mutation Application:**
"At each step, an item x∈𝒳 is sampled from the archive and modified by a mutation operator q:𝒳→𝒳, yielding a new item x′=q(x)."

## Three LLM-Guided Mutation Strategies

**Setting Mutator:**
Identifies underperforming categories and "prompts an LLM to rewrite a high-quality parent problem to match that category" while "the LLM is instructed to alter only the problem setting, leaving the reasoning structure and quantities unchanged."

**Distractor Mutator:**
"Adds semantically irrelevant sentences to a problem" that provide "additional detail or colour while preserving the original logic and solution."

**Symbolic Mutator:**
"Modifies the mathematical structure of the problem and updates the solution accordingly" via step-by-step reasoning generation.

## Empirical Results

**In-Distribution Performance (Table 1):**
- **Symbolic (GSM-Symbolic):** DéjàQ-S/A: 94.1±0.7% vs. Base 88.0±0.9%
- **P1 (harder in-distribution):** DéjàQ-S: 84.1±1.0% vs. Base 77.4±1.2%
- **P2 (hardest in-distribution):** DéjàQ-A: 65.5±1.9% vs. Base 62.6±1.9%

**Out-of-Distribution Performance:**
- **MATH-500:** DéjàQ-A: 69.6±4.0% vs. Base 68.0±4.1%
- **GPT-Eval-OOD:** DéjàQ-A: 89.0±2.7% vs. Base 86.6±3.0%

## Base Model and Problem Level

**Model:**
"Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (yang2024qwen25)" serves as both teacher (mutation proposer) and student (reasoning learner).

**Problem Source:**
Training initializes exclusively with "all templates from GSM-Symbolic" (based on GSM8K), representing grade-school level mathematics requiring 1–5 steps.

## Archive Evolution During Training

**Temporal Mechanisms:**
- **Mutation Depth Tracking:** "We track the mutation depth of each item and downweight the sampling probability of deeply mutated parents."
- **Periodic Refreshing:** "We periodically refresh a small fraction of archive cells by replacing their occupants with clean problem–answer pairs drawn from the seed dataset."
- **Score Decay:** "We apply exponential decay to stored learnability estimates and refresh them whenever the corresponding item appears in the GRPO batch."
- **BLEU Filtering:** "A mutated candidate is only considered for insertion if its surface form differs sufficiently from the parent" (threshold: 0.6).

## Critical Limitations

**Verifiability Degradation:**
Post-trained models exhibit concerning failure rates during mutation: "Base rates differ markedly across mutators: for the base model, DéjàQ-S yields 22.2%±2.9%, whereas DéjàQ-A yields 43.7%±3.4%" invalid problems. After post-training: "the rates shift to 35.7%±3.3% for DéjàQ-S and 36.6%±3.4% for DéjàQ-A."

**Teacher-Student Misalignment:**
The authors identify that "as the student becomes stronger, generating genuinely new and correct problems becomes increasingly difficult" because "our RLVR process optimises only the student's performance and never directly improves the teacher."

**Robustness Trade-off:**
DéjàQ-A underperforms on in-distribution benchmarks compared to DéjàQ-S, suggesting structural mutations reduce immediate task fit despite improving generalization.

**Computational Overhead:**
While "memory usage is stable," GPU utilization reaches only 51.7%±41.5%, and "runs with mutations were consistently slower" due to scheduling contention.

# MathForge: Technical Deep Dive

## DGPO (Difficulty-Aware Group Policy Optimization)

### Core Innovation: Two-Component Approach

**Difficulty-Balanced Group Advantage Estimation (DGAE)**
DGPO replaces GRPO's standard deviation normalization with Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD):
- GRPO uses: `A^GR,i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r)`
- DGPO uses: `A^DG,i = (r_i - mean(r)) / MAD(r)`

The mathematical breakthrough: Using MAD ensures "the total update magnitude for a single question" remains constant at G (group size), regardless of accuracy distribution. GRPO's update magnitude peaks at 50% accuracy and drops toward 0% or 100%, creating an imbalance that suppresses updates for harder questions.

**Difficulty-Aware Question-Level Weighting (DQW)**
Questions receive exponential weighting based on difficulty:
```
λ_s = B_v · exp(D_s/T) / Σexp(D_s/T)
where D_s = -mean({r_si})  [difficulty = negative mean reward]
T = 2.0 (temperature hyperparameter)
```

## MQR (Multi-Aspect Question Reformulation)

Three complementary reformulation strategies preserve the original answer while increasing difficulty:

1. **Background**: Adds unrelated narrative context requiring information filtering
2. **Term**: Introduces abstract mathematical terminology to test concept mastery
3. **Sub-Problem**: Converts numerical conditions into independent nested problems requiring cross-domain reasoning

Data augmentation expands dataset 4x (original + three reformulated versions).

## Experimental Results

### Primary Benchmark (Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH dataset):

| Benchmark | Base | GRPO | DGPO | MQR | MathForge | Improvement |
|-----------|------|------|------|-----|-----------|-------------|
| **AIME24** | 12.19 | 20.94 | 23.85 | 25.00 | **24.58** | +3.64 pts |
| **AIME25** | 4.79 | 8.44 | 10.21 | 11.77 | **12.60** | +4.16 pts |
| **AMC23** | 35.23 | 58.98 | 61.02 | 59.38 | **59.84** | +0.86 pts |
| **MATH500** | 48.60 | 72.20 | 74.25 | 77.85 | **79.95** | +7.75 pts |
| **Minerva** | 15.07 | 27.76 | 31.07 | 31.43 | **33.36** | +5.60 pts |
| **OlympiadBench** | 16.33 | 37.33 | 38.33 | 40.81 | **42.67** | +5.34 pts |
| **Average** | 22.04 | 37.61 | 39.79 (+2.18) | 41.04 (+3.43) | **42.17 (+4.56)** | +4.56 pts |

### Cross-Model Validation:

**Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B:**
- GRPO: 29.39% → MathForge: 33.84% (+4.45 pts)

**Qwen2.5-3B:**
- GRPO: 25.47% → MathForge: 29.01% (+3.54 pts)

**DeepSeek-Math-7B** (fine-tuned on 80k NuminaMath-CoT):
- GRPO: 14.91% → MathForge: 17.77% (+2.86 pts)

### Multimodal Domain (Qwen2.5-VL-3B on GeoQA):
- GRPO: 57.43% → DGPO: 59.95% (+2.52 pts)

## Base Models Used

- Qwen2.5-Math-7B (primary), 1.5B, 3B variants
- Qwen2.5-3B (general)
- DeepSeek-Math-7B
- Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (multimodal)
- Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B (for reformulation testing)

## Training Paradigm

**Offline Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR):**
- Uses rule-based accuracy rewards (binary: 1 for correct, 0 for incorrect)
- No neural reward models required
- Eliminates "reward hacking" risks
- Based on Open-R1 codebase using 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs

## Comparison to Vanilla GRPO

| Method | Mechanism | Average Score | Delta |
|--------|-----------|---------------|-------|
| **GRPO** | Baseline | 37.61 | — |
| **Dr.GRPO** | Removes length/objective bias | 37.40 | −0.21 |
| **GPG** | Critic-less, valid query filtering | 37.93 | +0.32 |
| **DAPO** | Advantage refinement at scale | 37.94 | +0.33 |
| **GSPO** | Alternative optimization objective | 37.71 | +0.10 |
| **GRPO-AD** | Difficulty-aware advantage reweighting | 38.26 | +0.65 |
| **DGPO** | MAD normalization + DQW | 39.79 | **+2.18** |
| **MQR (alone)** | Data augmentation with GRPO | 41.04 | **+3.43** |
| **MathForge** | DGPO + MQR combined | 42.17 | **+4.56** |

## Ablation Studies

**DGPO components** (Qwen2.5-Math-7B):
- Valid token-level averaging alone: +0.10 pts
- DGAE (MAD replacement) alone: +0.94 pts
- DQW alone: +1.14 pts
- Full DGPO: +2.18 pts

**Temperature sensitivity** (DQW):
- T=1.0: 39.03% (+1.42 pts)
- T=2.0: 39.79% (+2.18 pts) ← **optimal**
- T=5.0: 39.53% (+1.92 pts)
- T=10.0: 39.27% (+1.66 pts)

**MQR components**:
- Background reformulation: +1.05 pts
- Term reformulation: +1.34 pts
- Sub-Problem reformulation: +1.63 pts
- All three combined: +2.27 pts

## Key Findings

**Training Dynamics:**
- DGPO produces more concise outputs than GRPO while improving accuracy
- MQR shows "train harder, test better" phenomenon with consistently lower training accuracy but superior evaluation performance

**Difficulty Assessment:**
Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy on reformulated subsets:
- Original: 79.77%
- Background: 77.31%
- Term: 76.87%
- Sub-Problem: 72.04% (hardest)

**Reformulator Model Flexibility:**
- OpenAI o3: 42.17% average (+2.27 pts)
- Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking: 41.85% (+1.95 pts)
- Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 41.09% (+1.19 pts)

Demonstrates effectiveness across different reformulator capabilities.

## Limitations

While not explicitly stated, the paper implies:

1. **Computational overhead**: MQR requires a capable reformulation model (though smaller models work adequately)
2. **Answer preservation constraint**: Restricts reformulation flexibility to maintain original solutions
3. **Question difficulty metric**: Relies solely on mean accuracy; doesn't capture nuanced difficulty aspects
4. **Binary reward system**: Limited to problems with verifiable correct/incorrect answers
5. **Temperature sensitivity**: DQW performance depends on appropriate T tuning
6. **Scalability**: Tested primarily on 1.5B-7B models; behavior on larger models not explored

SPEED-RL introduces Selective Prompting with Efficient Estimation of Difficulty (SPEED), an adaptive online RL curriculum that selectively chooses training examples of intermediate difficulty to maximize learning efficiency. RLVR is a rapidly evolving paradigm for aligning LLMs through external reward verification, self-consistency, and bootstrap learning, enabling models to improve reasoning capabilities without relying heavily on human supervision.

Online Curriculum Learning assesses problem difficulty in real-time and guides an Adaptive Problem Restructuring mechanism to diversify medium problems and simplify hard ones, transforming the training process into a structured, adaptive curriculum that co-evolves with the model's capabilities.

A critical issue in RLVR involves maintaining both quality and diversity. RLVR has achieved substantial gains in single-attempt accuracy (Pass@1) on reasoning tasks, yet often suffers from reduced multi-sample coverage (Pass@K), indicating diversity collapse.

Diversity-Preserving Hybrid RL (DPH-RL) uses mass-covering f-divergences to mitigate diversity collapse in RLVR for LLMs, standing as a pivotal development that leverages f-divergences to maintain solution diversity and mitigate knowledge decay.

The paper "Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization: Breaking RLVR's Indifference to Diversity" addresses how Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) achieves gains in single-attempt accuracy (Pass@1) on reasoning tasks but often suffers from reduced multi-sample coverage (Pass@K), indicating diversity collapse.

The paper identifies that common RLVR objectives, such as GRPO, are indifferent to how probability mass is distributed among correct solutions. The paper was submitted on May 1, 2026 by Anamika Lochab, Bolian Li, and Ruqi Zhang from Purdue University's Department of Computer Science.
